clarifier-surface-loading.formula: SOR = flow x 1e6 / area (gpd/ft^2); weir = flow x 1e6 / weir_len (gpd/ft); solids = (flow + return sludge flow) x MLSS x 8.34 / area (lb/ft^2/day).
clarifier-surface-loading.edition: Clarifier surface, weir, and solids loading rates, standard wastewater-operations practice (Ten States Standards / Metcalf & Eddy), by name.
clarifier-surface-loading.freeAccess: The overflow-rate and solids-loading relations are standard published wastewater results; the state design criteria govern the limits.
clarifier-surface-loading.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
clarifier-surface-loading.editionNote: The clarifier loading checks: the surface overflow rate = flow / surface area (gpd/ft^2), the weir overflow rate = flow / total weir length (gpd/ft), and the secondary-clarifier solids loading = (flow + return sludge flow) x MLSS x 8.34 / area (lb/ft^2/day). Typical design ceilings are roughly 700-1000 gpd/ft^2 SOR, 10,000-20,000 gpd/ft weir, and 20-30 lb/ft^2/day solids; exceeding the SOR carries floc over the weir. This returns the rates for comparison; the Ten States Standards and the state design criteria govern the actual limits. An operations aid; the operator of record and the primacy agency govern.

assumptions.name: Surface overflow rate
assumptions.value: SOR = flow / surface area (gpd/ft^2)

assumptions.name: Weir and solids loading
assumptions.value: weir = flow / weir length; solids = (flow + return sludge flow) x MLSS x 8.34 / area

assumptions.name: Design limits
assumptions.value: state design criteria govern the actual ceilings

transformer-loading-efficiency.formula: output = kVA x load x pf; losses = (noload_w + load^2 x loadloss_w)/1000; efficiency = output/(output+losses); peak at load = sqrt(noload/loadloss).
transformer-loading-efficiency.edition: Transformer loading efficiency and losses, standard power-transformer practice (IEEE C57 loss definitions) by name; first-principles core-plus-copper loss model.
transformer-loading-efficiency.freeAccess: The core-plus-copper loss model and the efficiency relation are first-principles; transformer test-report losses are manufacturer data.
transformer-loading-efficiency.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
transformer-loading-efficiency.editionNote: A transformer has a fixed no-load (core / iron / excitation) loss that is present whenever it is energized, plus a load (copper / I^2R / winding) loss that varies with the square of the load fraction. Output kW = kVA x load fraction x power factor; total loss kW = (no-load loss + load^2 x full-load copper loss) / 1000; efficiency = output / (output + total loss). Peak efficiency occurs where the variable copper loss equals the fixed core loss, at a load fraction = sqrt(no-load / full-load loss), commonly 40-60% for a distribution transformer -- which is why a lightly loaded oversized transformer has a poor all-day (energy) efficiency even though its nameplate efficiency looks high. A design/screening aid; the manufacturer's certified test report governs the actual losses.

assumptions.name: Two-part loss
assumptions.value: fixed core loss + load^2 x full-load copper loss

assumptions.name: Efficiency
assumptions.value: output / (output + total loss), output = kVA x load x pf

assumptions.name: Peak load
assumptions.value: maximum efficiency at load = sqrt(no-load / full-load loss)

evaporative-cooling.formula: Cooling (Btu/hr) = water evaporated (lb/hr) x latent heat of vaporization h_fg (Btu/lb), default 1054 Btu/lb (water near 70-80 F; 970.3 is the 212 F value); tons = Btu/hr / 12,000.
evaporative-cooling.edition: ASHRAE Fundamentals psychrometrics by name; classical thermodynamics.
evaporative-cooling.freeAccess: Psychrometric formulas free in published engineering texts.
evaporative-cooling.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.

assumptions.name: Latent heat
assumptions.value: h_fg 1054 Btu/lb at typical evaporating temperatures unless the user supplies another; the supply-temperature effectiveness relations are in the evaporative-cooler tiles, not here

fastener-pullout.formula: Withdrawal capacity per inch of penetration: nails W = 1380 × G^2.5 × D; wood screws W = 2850 × G^2 × D (NDS 12.2); G is wood specific gravity, D is fastener shank diameter; lag screws are not modeled.
fastener-pullout.edition: AWC NDS-2018 (National Design Specification for Wood Construction). Chapter 12 (dowel-type fastener withdrawal).
fastener-pullout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed structural engineer govern.
fastener-pullout.editionNote: Editions available: AWC NDS-2024 is the current published edition (the one the 2024 IBC references); the withdrawal, bearing and C_V relations used here carry over from NDS-2018.

assumptions.name: Specific gravity table
assumptions.value: data/construction/lumber-properties.json keyed to species

tire-gearing.formula: Effective tire diameter from metric size (e.g., 285/75R17): D_in = (W_mm × ratio/100 × 2 + R_in × 25.4) / 25.4. Revs/mile = 63 360 / (π × D). Effective ratio = axle_ratio × (rev/mi_new / rev/mi_stock) x top gear -- a taller tire turns fewer revs per mile and LOWERS the effective ratio (3.73 to a 33 in tire reads about 3.57).
tire-gearing.edition: Tire & Rim Association (TRA) Yearbook by name; ETRTO Standards Manual by name; SAE J267 metric-tire size convention.
tire-gearing.freeAccess: TRA / ETRTO licensed; principles free at most tire-manufacturer technical pages (Goodyear, Michelin).
tire-gearing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tire-gearing.editionNote: Single-edition (TRA / ETRTO + SAE J267 size conventions).

drying-log.formula: Per reading: GPP = humidity-ratio * 7000 from temperature_F / RH via the bundled psychrometric helper. Boundary-pass: chamber_GPP < ambient_GPP. Trend: linear regression of chamber_GPP vs day_index (least-squares). Estimated days-to-target = (target - intercept) / slope - last_day, when slope is negative.
drying-log.edition: IICRC S500-2021 (Standard for Professional Water Damage Restoration). Public-domain boundary-humidity test method; IICRC governs acceptance.
drying-log.freeAccess: iicrc.org for TOC; full standard is licensed.
drying-log.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
drying-log.editionNote: Boundary-humidity test is a public method; the standard governs acceptance. Field instruments are the verdict; the calculator is a sanity envelope.

assumptions.name: Maximum readings
assumptions.value: 14 daily readings (one per day for a typical drying job)

assumptions.name: Default drying target
assumptions.value: ambient_GPP at the last reading minus 5 grains, when no explicit target is provided

assumptions.name: Trend model
assumptions.value: ordinary least-squares linear regression of chamber_GPP vs day_index

assumptions.name: Boundary failure
assumptions.value: chamber_GPP at or above ambient_GPP surfaces 'check equipment placement and exhaust per IICRC S500'

assumptions.name: Flat / rising trend
assumptions.value: non-negative slope warns 'drying is not progressing - re-evaluate the drying plan'

draft-lift-max.formula: theoretical_lift = 33.9 - site_elevation / 1000; attainable_lift = pump_factor x theoretical_lift - suction_losses (pump_factor about 2/3).
draft-lift-max.edition: IFSTA / NWCG firefighter math altitude-corrected drafting maximum lift, by name.
draft-lift-max.freeAccess: The drafting-lift relations are public fire-service / wildland training material; incident command governs the actual setup.
draft-lift-max.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
draft-lift-max.editionNote: 1 in Hg of vacuum is about 1.13 ft of lift. A real pump cannot pull a perfect vacuum, so about two-thirds of theoretical is the practical ceiling (about 22.5 ft at sea level), and every 1,000 ft of altitude takes about a foot off the theoretical lift (about two-thirds of a foot off the attainable). Lift is limited by atmospheric pressure pushing water up the suction, not the pump pulling it, so a bigger pump does not help; over the attainable lift you must resite the pump lower - a planning aid, not incident command.

assumptions.name: Practical ceiling
assumptions.value: about two-thirds of theoretical (about 22.5 ft at sea level); a perfect vacuum is unattainable

assumptions.name: Altitude correction
assumptions.value: theoretical lift falls about 1 ft per 1,000 ft of elevation

reverse-lay-friction.formula: One line: FL = C × Q² × L. n parallel lines sharing the flow: FL_per_line = FL_single / n², each carrying Q/n. (Pumps in tandem on one line share the single-line loss; they do not reduce it.)
reverse-lay-friction.edition: NFA hose-hydraulics training materials by name.
reverse-lay-friction.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.

assumptions.name: Equal flow split
assumptions.value: Q / n per parallel hose unless user supplies a measured imbalance

fire-alarm-nac-voltage-drop.formula: available_voltage_v = panel_min_output_v when given, else 0.85 x nominal_voltage_v (CUSTV); loop_R = 2 x run_length_ft x (resistance_per_1000ft / 1000); voltage_drop_v = total_current_a x loop_R; eol_voltage_v = available_voltage_v - voltage_drop_v; within_spec when eol >= device_min_v.
fire-alarm-nac-voltage-drop.edition: NFPA 72 (National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code) notification-appliance-circuit power / voltage provisions with the NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 conductor resistance, by name; the listed panel and appliances and the AHJ govern.
fire-alarm-nac-voltage-drop.freeAccess: The Ohm's-law voltage-drop relation is public physics; the starting voltage is the panel's listed minimum NAC output (0.85 x nominal is a common convention when none is listed), and the conductor ohms/1000 ft come from NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 (the appliance draws and listed minimums are on the datasheets).
fire-alarm-nac-voltage-drop.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fire-alarm-nac-voltage-drop.editionNote: A fire-alarm notification-appliance circuit (NAC) must deliver at least each horn/strobe's listed minimum voltage at the end of the line. The panel's usable output is not its nominal voltage but its regulated minimum output, the CUSTV, which the panel's installation manual lists (19.9 V or 20.4 V on a 24 V panel), or by common convention about 85% of nominal (20.4 V on a 24 V system). On a Class B (out-and-back) circuit the loop resistance is 2 x the one-way length x the conductor resistance per 1000 ft from NEC Chapter 9 Table 8. Lumping ALL the appliance current at the end of the line is the conservative worst case, giving V_EOL = CUSTV - I x loop_R, which must exceed the device's listed minimum (about 16 V for a 24 V appliance) with margin. When it fails the remedy is heavier conductors, a shorter run, splitting the circuit, or a NAC power extender / booster near the load. This is a design screen; the panel's actual regulated voltage, the appliance current draws and listed minimums, the wire table, and a stamped fire-alarm design and the AHJ govern the final circuit.

assumptions.name: CUSTV and Class B
assumptions.value: usable voltage = the panel's listed minimum NAC output, else 0.85 x nominal by convention; Class B loop = 2 x length x ohms/1000 ft
assumptions.source: panel installation manual / NEC Ch 9 Table 8

assumptions.name: Worst-case load
assumptions.value: total appliance current lumped at the end of the line; each device must still see its listed minimum

assumptions.name: Default conductor
assumptions.value: #14 stranded copper, 3.14 ohm/1000 ft at 75 C (3.07 solid)

hydraulic-reservoir-cooler.formula: hydraulic_hp = pump_gpm x pressure_psi / 1714; input_hp = hydraulic_hp / pump_efficiency; heat_hp = input_hp x heat_fraction; heat_btu_hr = heat_hp x 2545; reservoir_gal = pump_gpm x reservoir_multiplier; cooler_duty = max(0, heat_btu_hr - reservoir_dissipation).
hydraulic-reservoir-cooler.edition: Hydraulic power from gpm x psi / 1,714, the heat fraction of input power converted at 2,545 BTU/hr per horsepower, and the classic reservoir dwell-time rule of three times pump flow for industrial units (one to two for mobile), by name -- public fluid-power practice. The component manufacturers' published efficiencies, the duty cycle, and a measured oil temperature govern.
hydraulic-reservoir-cooler.freeAccess: The power and heat conversions are public physics; the efficiencies, heat fraction, and tank dissipation are the designer's own values.
hydraulic-reservoir-cooler.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydraulic-reservoir-cooler.editionNote: Everything a hydraulic system does that is not useful work becomes heat in the oil: pressure drop across valves and lines, relief-valve flow, and pump and motor inefficiency. A quarter of input power is a common working figure for a system with ordinary metering losses, and on a system that spends much of its cycle over relief it is considerably more, which is why the heat fraction is an input rather than a constant. The reservoir does three jobs -- de-aerate, settle contamination, and shed heat -- and the classic industrial rule of three times the pump's per-minute flow is really a dwell-time rule: it gives the oil about three minutes in the tank to release entrained air before it goes around again. Mobile equipment cannot carry that much oil and runs one to two times instead, which is exactly why mobile systems need coolers and industrial power units often do not. The last line is the design decision, and its consequence is worth stating plainly: whatever heat the reservoir cannot shed at the acceptable oil temperature, a cooler must, and if neither does it the oil temperature climbs until viscosity falls far enough that leakage losses balance the input. That is a stable equilibrium and a destructive one. Circuit design, not cooler selection, is where hydraulic heat is actually controlled.

assumptions.name: Heat fraction
assumptions.value: about 25% of input power for a system with ordinary metering losses; far more on one that lives over relief

assumptions.name: Reservoir rule
assumptions.value: 3x pump flow industrial, 1 to 2x mobile -- a dwell-time rule for de-aeration, not a heat rule

assumptions.name: If nothing rejects it
assumptions.value: oil temperature climbs until viscosity drops far enough that leakage balances input -- stable and destructive

terminal-velocity.formula: rho_mass = rho_weight/g; V_t = sqrt(2 W/(rho_mass Cd A)) (drag balances weight, W = 1/2 rho V^2 Cd A). g = 32.174 ft/s^2.
terminal-velocity.edition: The terminal-velocity balance W = 1/2 rho V^2 Cd A solved for V (standard fluid mechanics), by name; the drag-limited counterpart to free-fall-drop.
terminal-velocity.freeAccess: The terminal-velocity relation is a standard published fluid-mechanics result; the weight, frontal area, drag coefficient, and air density are the user's inputs.
terminal-velocity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
terminal-velocity.editionNote: Terminal velocity, the steady speed where the aerodynamic drag 1/2 rho V^2 Cd A exactly balances the weight W and the object stops accelerating: V_t = sqrt(2 W/(rho_mass Cd A)), with the mass air density rho_mass = (weight density)/g (g = 32.174 ft/s^2), the frontal area A, and the drag coefficient Cd. Heavy, compact, slick objects (small A, small Cd, big W) fall fast; light, bluff ones settle slowly. A 180 lb skydiver at 7 ft^2 and Cd 0.7 terminals at the familiar 120 mph. This is the CEILING that free-fall-drop (no drag) ignores - a compact tool over a short jobsite drop is still accelerating (free-fall is right), but a sheet of plywood or a person tops out and falls no faster no matter the height. The approach is not instant: from rest the speed follows v = Vt tanh(g t/Vt), reaching 95% of terminal after (Vt/g) atanh(0.95) seconds and (Vt^2/g) ln(1/sqrt(1 - 0.95^2)) feet of fall; tumbling that changes Cd and A, compressibility, and altitude density change are separate. Pair with free-fall-drop and aerodynamic-drag-force. A planning estimate; field conditions govern.

assumptions.name: Balance
assumptions.value: V_t = sqrt(2 W/(rho_mass Cd A)), drag equals weight at terminal

assumptions.name: Constant Cd
assumptions.value: steady terminal for a constant drag coefficient in still air

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: distance/time to reach terminal, tumbling, and altitude density change are separate

triangle-sss.formula: A = acos((b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2bc)) and likewise B, C; s = (a+b+c)/2; area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) (Heron). Triangle inequality required.
triangle-sss.edition: The law of cosines solved for the angles with Heron's area formula - first-principles plane trigonometry as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
triangle-sss.freeAccess: Pure plane trigonometry, public; the three sides are user-supplied measurements.
triangle-sss.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
triangle-sss.editionNote: Oblique-triangle solve from three measured sides (SSS). Each angle is the law of cosines, A = acos((b^2 + c^2 - a^2)/(2bc)) opposite side a and likewise for B and C, and the area is Heron's formula sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) with the semiperimeter s = (a+b+c)/2. A right angle (90 degrees) opposite the longest side means the corner is square - the framer's 3-4-5 tape check made general. The three sides must satisfy the triangle inequality (each less than the sum of the other two) or no triangle exists. The SAS case is triangle-sas, ASA is triangle-asa, and the ambiguous SSA is triangle-ssa. Plane triangles only. A layout aid; verify critical dimensions on the work.

assumptions.name: Law of cosines + Heron
assumptions.value: angles from acos((b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2bc)); area = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c))

assumptions.name: Triangle inequality
assumptions.value: each side must be less than the sum of the other two

fiber-loss-budget.formula: loss = attenuation(dB/km) * length_km + connectors * loss_per_connector + splices * loss_per_splice; margin = max_channel_loss - loss; pass when margin >= 0.
fiber-loss-budget.edition: Optical link loss budget - fiber attenuation plus connector and splice losses against the application's maximum channel loss - per the TIA-568 / TIA-526 fiber-test methods and the IEEE 802.3 channel-loss limits, by name; first-principles.
fiber-loss-budget.freeAccess: First-principles dB accounting. Attenuation coefficients and component losses are component-specific and user-supplied; the OTDR/power-meter field test governs the certified link.
fiber-loss-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed electrician govern. Verify against the NEC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
fiber-loss-budget.editionNote: TIA-568 / TIA-526 / IEEE 802.3. Multimode vs single-mode default coefficients are a labeled choice so a value is never read against the wrong fiber. Cross-links poe-budget.

assumptions.name: Component losses
assumptions.value: per-connector 0.75 dB and per-splice 0.3 dB defaults; user-supplied

paver-patio.formula: Pavers/sq ft = 144 / face area; pavers = ceil(area x pavers/sq ft x (1 + waste)); base/sand cu yd = area x depth(in) / 324.
paver-patio.edition: ICPI interlocking-paver base and bedding guidance (by name).
paver-patio.freeAccess: ICPI tech specs free at icpi.org.
paver-patio.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
paver-patio.editionNote: Single-edition (engineering-practice / first-principles take-off; refresh as practice and product data shift).

assumptions.name: Base depth band
assumptions.value: ~4-6 in walkway/patio, 8-12 in driveway, ~1 in bedding sand (editable)

recovery-cylinder.formula: specific_gravity = density(lb/gal) / 8.34; max_net = 0.80 x water_capacity x specific_gravity; remaining = max(0, max_net - current). Do not fill when current >= max_net.
recovery-cylinder.edition: DOT / AHRI 700 / EPA Section 608 recovery practice (by name).
recovery-cylinder.freeAccess: The 80% fill rule and the WC/tare basis are public refrigerant-handling practice.
recovery-cylinder.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
recovery-cylinder.editionNote: Single-edition (the cylinder stamp, the property sheet, and EPA 608 govern).

assumptions.name: Fill fraction
assumptions.value: 0.80 maximum (the 80% rule leaves room for liquid expansion with temperature); never fill past it

assumptions.name: Net basis
assumptions.value: water capacity (WC) and tare are stamped on the cylinder; net = gross on the scale minus tare; 8.34 lb per gallon water basis

assumptions.name: Handling
assumptions.value: never mix refrigerants; use only a cylinder rated and in-date for recovery; EPA Section 608 governs

blast-powder-factor.formula: loading density lb/ft = (pi / 4) x (diameter / 12) squared x 62.4 x explosive specific gravity; charge length = bench height + subdrill - stemming; charge weight = the product; rock tons per hole = burden x spacing x bench height x rock density / 2,000; powder factor = charge weight / tons.
blast-powder-factor.edition: The standard powder-factor relations by name, with 62.4 lb per cubic foot as the water reference an explosive's specific gravity is taken against and 2,000 lb per ton. Pattern and charge arithmetic only for a vertical hole with a single continuous column charge. Blasting is a licensed activity: the blaster in charge, the state and federal explosives regulations, MSHA or OSHA jurisdiction, and the site's blast plan govern.
blast-powder-factor.freeAccess: Geometry and density arithmetic on the user's own pattern and product data; no explosive manufacturer table is reproduced.
blast-powder-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
blast-powder-factor.editionNote: The pattern and the hole do the work together. Burden and spacing set how much rock a hole is responsible for; diameter and explosive density set how much energy is in it. Powder factor is just the ratio, and its value is that it is comparable across shots, benches, and years in a way that a stated pattern is not. The two lengths that do not appear in the pattern matter as much as the ones that do. Subdrilling below grade, typically a third of the burden, is what keeps the toe from being left high, and a shot that leaves toe costs more in secondary breakage than the extra drilling ever did. Stemming, typically about seven tenths of the burden, is what keeps the gases in the hole long enough to break rock instead of venting; short stemming is the direct cause of flyrock and airblast. Pushing the pattern out drops the powder factor and the cost per ton, and it is also the point at which fragmentation starts to suffer -- the loader notices before the spreadsheet does. The charge weight per hole is the number that goes into the vibration check, per DELAY rather than per shot. This does not design a blast, select an explosive, handle decked or bottom-loaded charges or air decks, or account for hole angle, and it does not predict fragmentation, which depends on rock structure, jointing, and initiation timing far more than on the ratio.

assumptions.name: Powder factor is comparable, a pattern is not
assumptions.value: which is why it is the number carried across shots and years

assumptions.name: Subdrill pays for itself
assumptions.value: a shot that leaves toe costs more in secondary breakage than the extra drilling

assumptions.name: Charge weight enters vibration PER DELAY
assumptions.value: not per shot, and the difference is enormous

flammable-cabinet-storage.formula: cabinets for Category 1-3 = ceil(gallons / 60); cabinets on the Category 4 limit = ceil((Category 1-3 + Category 4 gallons) / 120), since NFPA 30 9.5.3 makes 120 gal the cabinet total (the standard itself gives no blending rule); cabinets needed = the larger of the two; the area ceiling is 3 cabinets, so 180 gal of Category 1-3 or 360 gal of Category 4 per storage area.
flammable-cabinet-storage.edition: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.152(b)(3), a US federal regulation in the public domain, quoted directly. Quantities beyond what cabinets may hold go to specially constructed inside storage rooms under the same section.
flammable-cabinet-storage.freeAccess: 29 CFR is published in full at no cost by OSHA and the eCFR.
flammable-cabinet-storage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flammable-cabinet-storage.editionNote: The per-cabinet limit is the one everyone knows; the sentence that follows it is the one that decides a jobsite. Not more than THREE such cabinets may be located in a single storage area - which makes 180 gallons of Category 1-3 a hard ceiling for cabinet storage, not a starting point. You cannot buy your way past it with a fourth cabinet. Past that the standard sends you either to a genuinely separate storage area or to a specially constructed inside storage room, with fire-resistive construction, self-closing fire doors, a noncombustible sill or ramp, ventilation, and restricted electrical equipment - a building problem rather than a purchasing one, and far cheaper to discover while planning a site than while failing an inspection. The tile leads with that consequence rather than burying it under the cabinet count. On mixed contents the standard is genuinely silent: it states a limit for Category 1, 2 and/or 3 and a limit for Category 4, with no blending rule between them. The blend used here is NFPA 30 9.5.3's: 120 gallons is the cabinet's total, of which no more than 60 may be Category 1-3, so the requirement is the LARGER of the Category 1-3 count and the count on total gallons. That is stated explicitly, along with the note that an AHJ reading the OSHA caps as fractions of one cabinet that add would arrive at a higher number. One naming trap: the GHS-aligned categories replaced the older classes, so what older references call Class I and Class II is Categories 1, 2, and 3, and Class III is Category 4. A cabinet stencilled to the old scheme holds the same gallons. Not checked: cabinet approval, construction, labelling, and venting; container and portable tank sizes and approvals by category; quantities permitted OUTSIDE a cabinet in the work area, which are much smaller; separation from ignition sources, exits, and stairways; dispensing, bonding, and grounding; inside storage room construction; extinguisher provision; and state or local amendments, which on flammables are common. A screen, not a fire-protection plan; 1926.152, NFPA 30 as adopted, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Per cabinet
assumptions.value: 60 gal Category 1/2/3, or 120 gal Category 4

assumptions.name: Area ceiling
assumptions.value: not more than three cabinets in a single storage area

assumptions.name: Mixed contents
assumptions.value: no blending rule in 1926.152; NFPA 30 9.5.3's is used - 120 gal total per cabinet, at most 60 of it Category 1-3

assumptions.name: Beyond the ceiling
assumptions.value: a separate area or a specially constructed inside storage room, not a fourth cabinet

assumptions.name: Category naming
assumptions.value: Categories 1-3 are the old Class I and II; Category 4 is Class III

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: cabinet approval, container sizes, outside-cabinet quantities, ignition separation, dispensing

water-service-pressure-check.formula: a pressure-reducing valve is required where static pressure exceeds 80 psi; delivered pressure = the PRV setpoint where one is required and entered, otherwise the static pressure; headroom = delivered - the minimum fixture pressure; the system is CLOSED where a PRV is required or a check valve or backflow preventer is present; thermal expansion control is required where the system is closed AND a storage water heater is served.
water-service-pressure-check.edition: IPC 604.8 (static water pressure not greater than 80 psi, with an approved pressure-reducing valve conforming to ASSE 1003 or CSA B356 on the branch main or riser at the connection to the water service pipe where the main exceeds it) and IPC 607.3 (thermal expansion control where a storage water heater is supplied with cold water passing through a check valve, pressure-reducing valve, or backflow preventer, connected downstream of all such devices, and tanks sized so system pressure stays within 604.8).
water-service-pressure-check.freeAccess: Both are short prescriptive provisions widely reproduced in state adoptions and inspection guidance. No table is reproduced.
water-service-pressure-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
water-service-pressure-check.editionNote: The point of putting these two sections in one tile is that they form a chain people walk into one step at a time. High static pressure is a real defect rather than a comfort complaint - it splits supply lines, chews through fill valves and cartridges, and makes a house bang every time a solenoid closes - so 604.8 caps it at 80 psi and requires a pressure-reducing valve above that. Fitting the valve solves that problem and creates a new one, because the system is now CLOSED: heated water expands and has nowhere to push back to, so pressure climbs until the temperature and pressure relief valve weeps. 607.3 is what catches it, requiring a thermal expansion control device on a storage water heater's cold supply downstream of all check valves, pressure-reducing valves, and backflow preventers. The classic field sequence is someone fixing banging pipes with a PRV and, weeks later, wondering why the water heater started dripping - they completed a chain nobody told them existed, and a relief valve doing its job every day is not a solution. The subtler path is worth as much: a house at 65 psi needs no PRV on pressure grounds and STILL needs expansion control if a check valve or backflow preventer is on the service, which is why adding a backflow preventer for irrigation quietly triggers 607.3 on an existing house. The tile also separates static from flowing pressure explicitly, because headroom on paper is not headroom at the shower head once friction, elevation, and the meter come off it. Not checked: the expansion tank SIZE or precharge, which follows the manufacturer and the heater volume; per-fixture flow pressure and flow rate; pipe sizing and the losses between static and flowing pressure; seasonal and daily variation in service pressure, which is real; PRV maintenance and the fact that they tend to fail high; and the water heater's own relief valve and discharge piping. A screen; the adopted code, the device listings, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Pressure cap
assumptions.value: static water pressure not greater than 80 psi

assumptions.name: PRV
assumptions.value: required where the main exceeds 80 psi; ASSE 1003 or CSA B356

assumptions.name: Closed system
assumptions.value: a PRV, check valve, or backflow preventer all close it

assumptions.name: Expansion control
assumptions.value: required where a closed system serves a storage water heater, downstream of all such devices

assumptions.name: Static vs flowing
assumptions.value: headroom shown is static; friction, elevation, and the meter come off it under flow

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: tank size and precharge, per-fixture demand, pipe sizing, pressure variation, PRV failure modes

coefficient-of-consolidation.formula: Casagrande: cv = 0.197 Hdr^2 / t50. Taylor: cv = 0.848 Hdr^2 / t90. Hdr = H/2 (double) or H (single).
coefficient-of-consolidation.edition: The coefficient of consolidation cv from an oedometer (ASTM D2435) time-settlement curve by the Casagrande log-time and Taylor square-root-time fitting methods, as compiled in Das, Principles of Geotechnical Engineering / Holtz-Kovacs / Terzaghi, by name.
coefficient-of-consolidation.freeAccess: The Terzaghi time factors (T50 = 0.197, T90 = 0.848) and the cv = Tv Hdr^2/t relation are standard published soil-mechanics results; the fitting times t50/t90 are the user's own oedometer readings.
coefficient-of-consolidation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
coefficient-of-consolidation.editionNote: The coefficient of consolidation cv, the one input the consolidation-time-rate and consolidation-degree tiles require but the catalog did not otherwise produce, from an oedometer (ASTM D2435) time-settlement curve of a single load increment. Two standard curve-fitting methods: Casagrande's logarithm-of-time method reads the time t50 at 50% consolidation and gives cv = T50 Hdr^2/t50 with the theoretical time factor T50 = 0.197; Taylor's square-root-of-time method reads t90 at 90% and gives cv = T90 Hdr^2/t90 with T90 = 0.848. The drainage path Hdr is that of the small TEST SPECIMEN during the increment - half the specimen height for the usual two-way drainage (porous stones top and bottom), the full height for one-way - not the field layer thickness. cv varies with the stress level, so it is reported for several load increments; the two methods often disagree and Taylor tends to run higher. A design aid; the oedometer data and the geotechnical engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Drainage path
assumptions.value: Hdr = specimen height/2 (two-way) or full height (one-way)

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: one load increment; feeds the field consolidation-time tiles with the FIELD Hdr

cmu-wall-flexure.formula: n = Es/Em (Em = 900 f'm); rho = As/(b d); k = sqrt(2 rho n + (rho n)^2) - rho n; j = 1 - k/3; Ms = As Fs j d; Mm = 0.5 Fb k j b d^2 (Fb = 0.45 f'm); Ma = min(Ms, Mm).
cmu-wall-flexure.edition: TMS 402-16 (Building Code Requirements for Masonry Structures) allowable-stress-design cracked transformed-section flexure, as compiled in the Masonry Designers' Guide and CMHA TEK 14-07C, by name.
cmu-wall-flexure.freeAccess: CMHA TEK 14-07C (Allowable Stress Design of Concrete Masonry) is a free public CMHA technical note; the k / j working-stress arithmetic is public and printed in every masonry-design text.
cmu-wall-flexure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cmu-wall-flexure.editionNote: TMS 402-16 allowable-stress-design cracked transformed-section flexure: n = Es/Em with Es = 29,000,000 psi and Em = 900 f'm for concrete masonry, rho = As/(b d), k = sqrt(2 rho n + (rho n)^2) - rho n, j = 1 - k/3, the steel-governed allowable moment Ms = As Fs j d and the masonry-governed Mm = 0.5 Fb k j b d^2, with Fs = 32,000 psi for Grade 60 reinforcement and Fb = 0.45 f'm, as compiled in the Masonry Designers' Guide and CMHA TEK 14-07C. Returns the allowable service-level bending moment of a singly reinforced, fully grouted masonry section by the working-stress method: the section is assumed cracked, the reinforcement developed and in tension, the axial compression negligible (a wall in near-pure flexure), and one layer of steel at the reported effective depth. The axial term and the one-third stress increase are not applied, and this is not the strength-design (LRFD) moment. Take f'm, the bar size, and the spacing from the structural drawings. A design aid, not a substitute for the engineer of record's stamped design - the structural engineer of record's stamped design governs.

assumptions.name: Cracked working-stress section
assumptions.value: singly reinforced, fully grouted, cracked transformed section in near-pure flexure; the axial interaction and the slender-wall P-delta method are separate analyses

assumptions.name: Allowable stresses
assumptions.value: Fs = 32,000 psi (Grade 60) and Fb = 0.45 f'm, with Em = 900 f'm for concrete masonry; editable for other grades and materials

assumptions.name: Governing mode reported
assumptions.value: the lesser of the steel- and masonry-governed moments governs; adding steel past the balance point stops paying off once Mm < Ms

rtk-error-budget.formula: horizontal error = the fixed component + the ppm component x the baseline in km; vertical the same with its own coefficients, and roughly twice the horizontal; a base position error ADDS directly to both rather than combining in quadrature, because it is systematic.
rtk-error-budget.edition: The RTK error budget convention by name. The vertical is about twice the horizontal because satellites are all above the receiver and none below. A BASE POSITION ERROR IS SYSTEMATIC: every rover observation of the session inherits it exactly, it does not average out, and it does not appear in the data collector's internal quality figures. A float solution is not survey grade. A precision budget, not an accuracy statement: multipath, dilution of precision, ionospheric activity and geoid model uncertainty are not included. The receiver manufacturer's specification, the project's accuracy requirements, the control network, and the surveyor of record govern.
rtk-error-budget.freeAccess: One multiplication on a manufacturer's published specification; no receiver data is reproduced.
rtk-error-budget.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rtk-error-budget.editionNote: The fixed component is the receiver's own floor and does not improve with a shorter baseline; the ppm term grows with distance because the atmosphere the correction models diverges between the two receivers. The vertical is roughly twice the horizontal for a geometric reason rather than an electronic one: satellites are all above the receiver, so the intersection that fixes a horizontal position from many directions has only one side to work with vertically. THE FAILURE THAT DWARFS BOTH IS THE BASE POSITION -- a base set on an autonomous position can be off by a metre, and every rover observation of that session inherits it exactly. It is systematic, it does not average out, and it does not appear in the quality figures the data collector displays, which describe the vector from the base and not the base itself.

assumptions.name: A precision budget, not accuracy
assumptions.value: multipath, DOP, ionosphere and geoid uncertainty are excluded

assumptions.name: Base error adds, it does not combine
assumptions.value: it is a systematic shift on every observation of the session

assumptions.name: Only a fixed solution carries the specification
assumptions.value: a float solution stores coordinates that look identical in the file

walk-in-door-infiltration.formula: door open factor = openings per hour x seconds open / 3,600; effective airflow = the fully-open doorway flow x that factor x the doorway protection factor; load = airflow x 60 x air density x the enthalpy difference; latent load = the same mass flow x the moisture difference x 1,061 Btu/lb.
walk-in-door-infiltration.edition: The walk-in doorway infiltration relations by name. The fully-open doorway flow comes from the ASHRAE doorway flow relations or the manufacturer's data for the door size and temperature difference, and the enthalpy and moisture differences from a psychrometric chart at the two conditions. Protection factors (the share that still gets through) run about 0.05 for new strip curtains, rising to 0.15 to 0.2 as they wear (ASHRAE Refrigeration ch. 24: effectiveness 0.95 new, 0.8 to 0.85 in service), and 0.3 or more for an air curtain; ASHRAE also applies a doorway flow factor of 0.8 above an 11 C (20 F) difference, which the full-open airflow entered here should carry. It does not size the refrigeration system. ASHRAE's refrigeration handbook, the box and door manufacturer's data, and the refrigeration designer govern.
walk-in-door-infiltration.freeAccess: One fraction and two multiplications on a doorway flow and a psychrometric difference the reader supplies; no ASHRAE table is reproduced.
walk-in-door-infiltration.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
walk-in-door-infiltration.editionNote: The door open factor is simply the fraction of the hour the door stands open, and it is where a busy kitchen diverges from a design assumption: sixty openings of twenty seconds is a third of the hour, and a door propped for a delivery is all of it. On an ordinary box the door load at that duty commonly rivals the product and transmission loads combined. A large share of the load on a freezer door is LATENT, and that share has consequences beyond the compressor: the moisture condenses and freezes on the evaporator, which blocks airflow, raises the defrost frequency, and puts the defrost heat back into the box each cycle. Doorway protection is the cheapest intervention on the list, and cutting infiltration cuts the frost accumulation by roughly the same fraction.

assumptions.name: The doorway airflow is entered
assumptions.value: it depends on door height, density ratio and flow regime

assumptions.name: Steady state, not per-opening transient
assumptions.value: the air curtain re-establishment and doorway mixing are not modelled

assumptions.name: Not a refrigeration load calculation
assumptions.value: transmission, product, lighting, motor, personnel and defrost loads sit alongside this one

containment-bypass-airflow.formula: IT airflow = IT kW x 3,412/(1.08 x equipment delta-T); bypass = supply - IT airflow; mixed return follows the sensible heat balance; fan power varies with airflow cubed.
containment-bypass-airflow.edition: First-principles airflow mixing and the fan affinity laws, with ASHRAE TC 9.9 thermal guidance. Rack-level inlet surveys and commissioning measurements govern.
containment-bypass-airflow.freeAccess: Mass/heat balance plus the public cube-law fan relation.
containment-bypass-airflow.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
containment-bypass-airflow.editionNote: A positive arithmetic bypass is not proof that every rack is supplied: local recirculation and bypass can coexist. The failure cases are aggregate screens; room geometry, control response, and rack inlet measurements decide resilience.

assumptions.name: Uniform equipment rise
assumptions.value: all IT airflow is represented by one entered delta-T

assumptions.name: Fan affinity
assumptions.value: variable-speed fan power scales with the cube of airflow

ibu-tinseth.edition: Tinseth's empirical utilization fit. The brewery's own measured IBU (ASBC Beer-23) on its own system governs.
ibu-tinseth.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
ibu-tinseth.editionNote: Utilization rises fastest early, so a quarter of the boil gives about half the bitterness; wort gravity suppresses it, so a strong beer needs a bigger hop bill to taste the same.

assumptions.name: Fit
assumptions.value: an empirical fit to measured beers; whirlpool and late additions are not modelled
